commits.messageBody:
send_files() opened a pipe for every file at once, with no bound and no way
for a caller to set one, so uploading 500 files opened 500 concurrent pipes.
Same defect as #1381, fixed for the TypeScript client in #1716.

- add max_concurrent (default 5), validated before any pipe is opened
- replace the gather-every-coroutine call with a fixed worker pool; results
  keep the order of the files argument and per-file failures stay isolated
- drop the "Server handles queuing automatically" claim from the docstring
  and the two inline comments that repeated it

Fixes #1841
commits.messageHeadline: fix(client-python): bound send_files() concurrency with max_concurrent

commits.messageBody:
A file whose write() failed after open() left its pipe open on the server
while the worker moved on, so the batch could hold more than max_concurrent
pipes — the bound this change is meant to establish. Mirrors the cleanup
send() already does on its own error path.

The fake pipe in the tests grew is_opened and DataPipe's double-close guard
so it exercises the real close path.

Addresses CodeRabbit review on #1895.
commits.messageHeadline: fix(client-python): close the pipe when an upload fails mid-transfer

commits.messageBody:
stats['active'] == 0 only proved cleanup ran by the end of the batch. The
peak check proves the limit was never breached while the failure was in
flight, which is the property the leak actually broke: against the
pre-cleanup commit it reports 3 concurrent pipes against a limit of 2.
commits.messageHeadline: test(client-python): assert the bound holds on the write-failure path

commits.messageBody:
close() is the finalize call, not an abort - it flushes what was written and
commits it as a finished object. Closing a file that died mid-transfer
therefore ingested a truncated document, and since request() has no default
timeout it could also block a slot indefinitely. There is no abort
subcommand, so an interrupted pipe is left to the server zombie reaper,
which drops it without processing and releases its slot.

Replace the hand-rolled worker pool with asyncio.Semaphore. Same bound, less
code, and it restores the return_exceptions=True the pool had dropped.

The event body re-stat'd the file after the guarded block - a TOCTOU against
the exists() check, and the only statement outside the block that could
raise, so a file deleted mid-batch left results[index] as None. Reuse the
file_size already computed inside the block.
commits.messageHeadline: fix(client-python): stop finalizing pipes for interrupted uploads

commits.messageBody:
The agent API reference still said uploads are unbounded and that the server
handles queuing and rate limiting. That is the file agents are pointed at
before writing RocketRide code, so a bulk-ingest script written from it would
omit max_concurrent.

upload_time now covers the upload alone rather than including the wait for a
free slot, so note that on the field.
commits.messageHeadline: docs(client-python): correct the stale send_files concurrency claims

commits.messageBody:
upload_parser has carried a --threads flag commented "Thread configuration
for concurrent uploads" since before this change, and the agent reference
tells readers to "use --threads to control concurrency" - but it only ever
reached client.use(), so it set the pipeline thread count and nothing else.
On the --token path, where no pipeline is started, it did nothing at all.

Pass it to send_files() as max_concurrent. That is the same number the
server sizes its own pipe semaphore from (threads -> taskConfig.threadCount
-> Semaphore), so the client stops guessing 5 and matches the capacity that
is actually there, and the documented behaviour becomes true.
commits.messageHeadline: fix(client-python): honour --threads when uploading from the CLI

commits.messageBody:
…flag

The previous commit routed --threads into send_files, which made the same
flag mean two different things across the two CLIs: the TypeScript one has
--threads for pipeline execution and --max-concurrent for upload fan-out.
Match it. --threads goes back to only sizing the pipeline when the command
starts one, and --max-concurrent (default 5) bounds the uploads.

The value is checked at parse time so a bad limit fails before a pipeline
is started, same as the TypeScript CLI does.
commits.messageHeadline: fix(client-python): give the upload command its own --max-concurrent …
